[THOUGHT] The neonate presents with classic features of a distal neonatal intestinal obstruction: bilious vomiting and failure to pass meconium since birth, progressive abdominal distension, tympanic percussion, decreased bowel sounds, and dilated bowel loops on abdominal radiograph with absence of rectal gas. The diagnostic rectal biopsy demonstrates absence of ganglion cells in both the submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses, which is the pathological hallmark and gold-standard confirmation of congenital aganglionosis. While differential diagnoses for neonatal distal obstruction include meconium ileus (cystic fibrosis), intestinal atresia, or malrotation with volvulus, the biopsy finding definitively identifies an aganglionic segment causing functional obstruction. Therefore the single most likely diagnosis is congenital aganglionic megacolon (Hirschsprung disease).

Rectal biopsy is the gold standard diagnostic test; the described histopathology is diagnostic. Potential items that could be clarified but are not required to establish the diagnosis include biopsy technique (suction vs full‑thickness), adequacy/depth of the specimen, and whether ancillary stains (acetylcholinesterase or calretinin) were performed. Also useful for management would be extent of aganglionosis (contrast enema or intraoperative mapping), but these are not necessary to confirm the diagnosis. No immediate “red‑flag” test is missing for establishing the diagnosis itself.
